title: HTTP & Authentication
goal: Understand authentication without relying on framework magic.

topics.title: HTTP request
topics.description: An HTTP request names a target and method, carries metadata in headers, and may contain a body.
learningGoals: Method, path, metadata, and body are distinguished
Malformed input has a defined response
examples: POST /login carries JSON credentials.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: An HTTP request names a target and method, carries metadata in headers, and may contain a body. Parse each part under an explicit contract. Authentication, validation, and business behavior are separate decisions even when triggered by one request.

workedExample.scenario: POST /login carries JSON credentials.
steps: Content-Type identifies the body format.
The server validates the shape before authenticating.

commonMistakes: A well-formed request is not necessarily authorized or valid business input.
material.independentExercise: Write a reservation request contract with required and optional fields.
recallQuestions: Which information belongs in headers?
What must be checked before domain work?

acceptanceCriteria: Method, path, metadata, and body are distinguished
Malformed input has a defined response

topics.title: HTTP response
topics.description: A response reports the outcome of the request using a status, headers, and an optional representation.
learningGoals: Success and failure responses follow their contracts
Secrets and internal traces are excluded
examples: A session creation succeeds.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A response reports the outcome of the request using a status, headers, and an optional representation. Define stable success and failure shapes without exposing stack traces or secrets. Transport success should accurately reflect the promised operation.

workedExample.scenario: A session creation succeeds.
steps: Return the chosen success status and response data.
Set cookies in headers rather than embedding them as ordinary JSON metadata.

commonMistakes: Returning status 200 for every failure makes clients guess the result.
guidedExercise: Describe one success and rejection response
material.independentExercise: Create a consistent response contract for coupon creation and redemption.
recallQuestions: What does the status communicate?
What information must never appear?

acceptanceCriteria: Success and failure responses follow their contracts
Secrets and internal traces are excluded

topics.title: Headers
topics.description: Headers describe message metadata and request context.
learningGoals: Header trust assumptions are documented
Sensitive values are not logged
examples: A request supplies a correlation ID and Authorization.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Headers describe message metadata and request context. Names are case-insensitive; values follow their specific field rules. Client-supplied IDs, forwarding headers, and content types are untrusted unless a controlled boundary validates them.

workedExample.scenario: A request supplies a correlation ID and Authorization.
steps: Validate or replace the correlation value.
Never copy credentials into logs.

commonMistakes: Every incoming header is not trustworthy just because a proxy usually sends it.
guidedExercise: Identify values that should be redacted
material.independentExercise: Describe trusted-proxy handling for forwarded client metadata.
recallQuestions: Which headers can a client forge?
Which values require a size or format limit?

acceptanceCriteria: Header trust assumptions are documented
Sensitive values are not logged

topics.title: Cookies
topics.description: Cookies are stored and automatically attached by the browser according to scope and attributes.
learningGoals: Attributes match the deployment and threat model
Logout clears the intended cookie
examples: A refresh cookie is HttpOnly and Secure.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Cookies are stored and automatically attached by the browser according to scope and attributes. HttpOnly limits script access, Secure restricts transport, and SameSite affects cross-site sending. Each addresses a different risk and does not replace server-side validation.

workedExample.scenario: A refresh cookie is HttpOnly and Secure.
steps: The browser can still send it automatically.
The server must validate token and CSRF policy.

commonMistakes: HttpOnly does not make an application immune to XSS or CSRF.
material.independentExercise: Design creation and clearing of a refresh cookie using matching scope.
recallQuestions: What does HttpOnly prevent?
Why must logout clearing match cookie scope?

acceptanceCriteria: Attributes match the deployment and threat model
Logout clears the intended cookie

topics.title: Authorization header
topics.description: Authorization carries credentials under a defined scheme.
learningGoals: Malformed credentials cannot bypass validation
Credentials are never included in diagnostics
examples: Authorization contains Bearer plus an access token.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Authorization carries credentials under a defined scheme. Parse missing, malformed, and unsupported forms explicitly. Sending a credential is only the start: the server must validate it and check whether the authenticated principal may perform the operation.

workedExample.scenario: Authorization contains Bearer plus an access token.
steps: Validate the token.
Check ownership of the requested session.

commonMistakes: A bearer header does not prove the token is valid or the action authorized.
material.independentExercise: Compare cookie-based refresh with explicit access-token headers.
recallQuestions: What if the header is missing?
What checks remain after parsing?

acceptanceCriteria: Malformed credentials cannot bypass validation
Credentials are never included in diagnostics

topics.title: Status codes
topics.description: Choose status codes by the outcome and HTTP semantics.
learningGoals: Status and error body agree
Different failure categories are distinguishable
examples: A stale version prevents an update.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Choose status codes by the outcome and HTTP semantics. Separate malformed input, missing authentication, forbidden actions, conflicts, and server failures. A code alone is insufficient when the client needs a stable machine-readable failure reason.

workedExample.scenario: A stale version prevents an update.
steps: Return the documented conflict outcome.
Let the client distinguish it from invalid JSON.

commonMistakes: Status codes are not arbitrary domain error labels.
guidedExercise: Map five API outcomes to responses
material.independentExercise: Create a failure table for coupon endpoints.
recallQuestions: Which failures can a client fix?
How does a client identify a business conflict?

acceptanceCriteria: Status and error body agree
Different failure categories are distinguishable

topics.title: HTTP methods and idempotency

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: HTTP methods carry defined semantics.
learningGoals: Methods match their intended effects
Duplicate and retry behavior is stated
examples: Repeat DELETE for a revoked session.

material.explanation: HTTP methods carry defined semantics. Safe methods should not intentionally change server state; idempotent methods have the same intended effect after repetition, even if responses differ. A POST may support application-level idempotency through an explicit contract.

workedExample.scenario: Repeat DELETE for a revoked session.
steps: The session remains revoked.
The second response may differ without adding another effect.

commonMistakes: Idempotency means stable intended effect, not identical response bytes.
guidedExercise: Compare GET, PUT, POST, and DELETE
material.independentExercise: Design a refund POST with an idempotency-key contract.
recallQuestions: Can a response differ for an idempotent operation?
Why should GET not perform logout?

acceptanceCriteria: Methods match their intended effects
Duplicate and retry behavior is stated

topics.title: JSON contracts and validation

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: A JSON contract specifies field names, types, required values, and handling of unknown fields.
learningGoals: Invalid shapes are rejected at the boundary
Response fields do not leak internal models
examples: Register expects email and password strings.

material.explanation: A JSON contract specifies field names, types, required values, and handling of unknown fields. Validate structure before invoking domain behavior, then enforce domain rules at their owner. Avoid exposing persistence entities as an accidental public contract.

workedExample.scenario: Register expects email and password strings.
steps: Reject an array or missing password.
Apply domain and credential policy after shape validation.

commonMistakes: Valid JSON syntax does not imply valid request data.
material.independentExercise: Design a stable coupon request DTO without internal storage fields.
recallQuestions: What differs between structural and domain validation?
What can a contract change break?

acceptanceCriteria: Invalid shapes are rejected at the boundary
Response fields do not leak internal models

topics.title: API pagination and error contracts

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: API pagination needs bounded page sizes and a stable traversal contract.
learningGoals: Pagination limits and ordering are explicit
Clients can distinguish errors without parsing prose
examples: List a user's sessions with a cursor.

material.explanation: API pagination needs bounded page sizes and a stable traversal contract. Errors should provide a stable code and useful safe detail. Clients should not parse human prose to decide whether to retry or correct input.

workedExample.scenario: List a user's sessions with a cursor.
steps: Bound the requested limit.
Return a next cursor only when another page exists.

commonMistakes: Allowing arbitrary page sizes can make a simple endpoint expensive.
material.independentExercise: Test invalid cursor, maximum limit, and an empty page.
recallQuestions: What information makes a cursor stable?
Which error fields should clients depend on?

acceptanceCriteria: Pagination limits and ordering are explicit
Clients can distinguish errors without parsing prose

topics.title: Bearer token
topics.description: A bearer token grants the holder its associated authority when valid.
learningGoals: Exposure paths are identified
Authority and lifetime are deliberately limited
examples: A stolen valid access token is presented.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A bearer token grants the holder its associated authority when valid. Protect it in transit, storage, and logs; possession does not establish whether the rightful user supplied it. Keep scope, expiration, and resource access checks explicit.

workedExample.scenario: A stolen valid access token is presented.
steps: The server verifies its validity.
The token's limited lifetime and authority constrain exposure.

commonMistakes: A valid bearer token does not prove the caller is its original owner.
material.independentExercise: Document the lifecycle and redaction policy for an access token.
recallQuestions: What does possession prove?
What limits damage after disclosure?

acceptanceCriteria: Exposure paths are identified
Authority and lifetime are deliberately limited

topics.title: Session authentication
topics.description: Session authentication associates an unpredictable identifier with server-side state.
learningGoals: Session state is checked before protected work
One-session and all-session revocation differ
examples: Session S1 belongs to U1.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Session authentication associates an unpredictable identifier with server-side state. Validate that state on use and define expiration and revocation. Session storage introduces lifecycle and lookup decisions that differ from purely self-contained token checks.

workedExample.scenario: Session S1 belongs to U1.
steps: An authenticated request resolves S1.
Revoking S1 makes later session checks fail.

commonMistakes: A session identifier should not encode predictable user identity alone.
material.independentExercise: Design session revocation across two browser sessions.
recallQuestions: Where is authority stored?
What happens after revocation?

acceptanceCriteria: Session state is checked before protected work
One-session and all-session revocation differ

topics.title: Authentication and authorization

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Authentication establishes a principal; authorization decides what that principal may do.
learningGoals: Cross-user resource access is rejected
Authorization uses trusted principal data
examples: U1 requests revocation of U2's session.

material.explanation: Authentication establishes a principal; authorization decides what that principal may do. Deny unauthorized access even when credentials are valid, and check resource ownership on each relevant request rather than trusting a supplied user ID.

workedExample.scenario: U1 requests revocation of U2's session.
steps: Authenticate U1 successfully.
Reject the action because U1 does not own that session.

commonMistakes: A valid login is not permission to access every resource.
material.independentExercise: Design logout-all so the caller cannot choose another user's identity.
recallQuestions: Which question does authentication answer?
Where is resource ownership checked?

acceptanceCriteria: Cross-user resource access is rejected
Authorization uses trusted principal data

topics.title: JWT
topics.description: A JWT is a structured token; a signed JWT's payload is typically readable.
learningGoals: Unsigned or invalidly signed tokens are rejected
Revocation limitations are documented
examples: An access JWT names U1 and an expiry.

tasks.title: Explain JWT in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A JWT is a structured token; a signed JWT's payload is typically readable. Validate allowed algorithms, signature, issuer, audience, and time claims under your contract. Offline validity checking means server-side revocation is not automatically immediate.

workedExample.scenario: An access JWT names U1 and an expiry.
steps: Decode only to inspect it.
Trust claims only after complete validation.

commonMistakes: Decoding a token is not verifying it.
guidedExercise: Distinguish readable claims from trusted claims
material.independentExercise: Explain logout behavior when an already-issued JWT remains unexpired.
recallQuestions: Which claims must be validated?
Why can logout leave a JWT temporarily valid?

acceptanceCriteria: Unsigned or invalidly signed tokens are rejected
Revocation limitations are documented

topics.title: Opaque token
topics.description: An opaque token has no client-readable business meaning and should be generated unpredictably.
learningGoals: Raw tokens are not persisted or logged
Lookup leads to explicit server-side state
examples: A random refresh value maps to token row X through its hash.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: An opaque token has no client-readable business meaning and should be generated unpredictably. The server resolves it to state, preferably through a stored hash for high-entropy tokens. This allows explicit rotation, expiry, and revocation decisions.

workedExample.scenario: A random refresh value maps to token row X through its hash.
steps: The row identifies session and expiration.
Raw token storage is unnecessary for lookup.

commonMistakes: Base64 encoding a user ID does not make a secure opaque token.
guidedExercise: Separate raw secret from token identifier
material.independentExercise: Design token-table fields without raw secret persistence.
recallQuestions: Where does the token's meaning live?
Why should the value be unpredictable?

acceptanceCriteria: Raw tokens are not persisted or logged
Lookup leads to explicit server-side state

topics.title: Secure randomness

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Security tokens require an unpredictable random source and enough entropy for their threat model.
learningGoals: A cryptographically suitable source is used
Tests check format and secret-handling behavior
examples: Generate random bytes with SecureRandom.

material.explanation: Security tokens require an unpredictable random source and enough entropy for their threat model. Encode random bytes for transport without reducing their randomness. Do not substitute timestamps, counters, or ordinary pseudo-random generators.

workedExample.scenario: Generate random bytes with SecureRandom.
steps: Encode them using a transport-safe encoding.
Persist only the verification representation.

commonMistakes: An encoded predictable value is still predictable.
material.independentExercise: Design a token generator contract and test format without trying to prove security statistically.
recallQuestions: Does encoding add entropy?
What can a unit test prove about a generator?

acceptanceCriteria: A cryptographically suitable source is used
Tests check format and secret-handling behavior

topics.title: Hashing
topics.description: A hash maps input to a digest and does not provide reversible encryption.
learningGoals: Password and token policies are distinct
Raw values remain outside storage and logs
examples: Hash a random refresh token for lookup.

tasks.title: Explain Hashing in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A hash maps input to a digest and does not provide reversible encryption. High-entropy random token lookup differs from password storage: passwords need a deliberately expensive password-hashing scheme. Choose algorithms by the secret's threat model.

workedExample.scenario: Hash a random refresh token for lookup.
steps: A matching presented token yields the same digest.
Do not reuse that simple digest policy for human passwords.

commonMistakes: One hashing policy does not suit every kind of secret.
material.independentExercise: Document algorithm and encoding boundaries for token hashing.
recallQuestions: Why are password guesses different from random-token guesses?
What does a digest not protect against?

acceptanceCriteria: Password and token policies are distinct
Raw values remain outside storage and logs

topics.title: Password hashing

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Passwords are low-entropy human secrets, so use a vetted password-hashing implementation with salt and suitable cost.
learningGoals: Raw passwords are never persisted or logged
A vetted password-hashing scheme performs verification
examples: Two users choose the same password.

material.explanation: Passwords are low-entropy human secrets, so use a vetted password-hashing implementation with salt and suitable cost. OWASP favors modern password-hashing schemes such as Argon2id. Store the encoded verifier and support policy upgrades without inventing cryptography.

workedExample.scenario: Two users choose the same password.
steps: Unique salts produce different stored verifiers.
Verification uses the library's matching operation.

commonMistakes: A fast general-purpose digest is not adequate password storage.
guidedExercise: Use a supported verifier API in a small test
material.independentExercise: Design login verification and a safe rehash-on-success policy.
recallQuestions: What does a salt prevent?
Why must password hashing be intentionally costly?

acceptanceCriteria: Raw passwords are never persisted or logged
A vetted password-hashing scheme performs verification

topics.title: Encryption
topics.description: Encryption protects confidentiality by making data recoverable only with appropriate keys.
learningGoals: Encryption is chosen only for a reversible need
Key ownership and lifecycle are specified
examples: An encrypted backup requires a key to recover data.

tasks.title: Explain Encryption in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Encryption protects confidentiality by making data recoverable only with appropriate keys. Its mode, nonce rules, and key management matter; encoding provides no confidentiality. Use vetted libraries and avoid designing an encryption protocol as a beginner exercise.

workedExample.scenario: An encrypted backup requires a key to recover data.
steps: A digest cannot restore that data.
A signature answers a different question.

commonMistakes: Encryption does not automatically provide authenticity in every construction.
guidedExercise: Identify who needs the decryption key
material.independentExercise: Write a threat model for storing a recoverable third-party credential.
recallQuestions: When must a secret be recoverable?
What happens if the key is exposed?

acceptanceCriteria: Encryption is chosen only for a reversible need
Key ownership and lifecycle are specified

topics.title: Signing
topics.description: A digital signature verifies that content was authorized by the holder of a signing key and has not been changed.
learningGoals: Content secrecy is not assumed
Key trust and algorithm policies are explicit
examples: A JWT payload contains a public subject claim.

tasks.title: Explain Signing in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A digital signature verifies that content was authorized by the holder of a signing key and has not been changed. It does not hide the content. Verification depends on trusted key distribution and an explicit algorithm policy.

workedExample.scenario: A JWT payload contains a public subject claim.
steps: Changing the claim invalidates a valid signature.
Reading the unchanged claim requires no decryption.

commonMistakes: Signed does not mean encrypted or confidential.
guidedExercise: Compare readable payload and verified payload
material.independentExercise: Explain access-token key rotation and accepted-key overlap.
recallQuestions: What does verification establish?
How does the verifier trust a key?

acceptanceCriteria: Content secrecy is not assumed
Key trust and algorithm policies are explicit

topics.title: CSRF
topics.description: CSRF exploits automatically attached credentials to trigger actions from another site.
learningGoals: Cross-site unauthorized actions are rejected
The defense matches the credential transport
examples: A hostile page tries a cookie-authenticated POST.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: CSRF exploits automatically attached credentials to trigger actions from another site. Apply defenses appropriate to your browser and credential flow, such as CSRF tokens and origin checks. SameSite helps but should be evaluated alongside the entire request contract.

workedExample.scenario: A hostile page tries a cookie-authenticated POST.
steps: The browser may attach cookies under applicable rules.
The server rejects a missing or invalid CSRF proof.

commonMistakes: CORS alone is not a universal CSRF defense.
guidedExercise: Choose a defense for refresh and logout
material.independentExercise: Design and test a cookie-authenticated state-changing request policy.
recallQuestions: Which credentials are attached automatically?
Where is CSRF proof validated?

acceptanceCriteria: Cross-site unauthorized actions are rejected
The defense matches the credential transport

topics.title: XSS
topics.description: XSS lets attacker-controlled script execute in a trusted origin.
learningGoals: Untrusted content is not executed as markup
Credential-exposure risks are explained
examples: A note contains HTML with a script payload.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: XSS lets attacker-controlled script execute in a trusted origin. Escape output for its context, avoid unsafe HTML insertion, and use defense in depth. HttpOnly reduces direct cookie reads but malicious script may still perform actions as the user.

workedExample.scenario: A note contains HTML with a script payload.
steps: Render it as text.
Do not interpret it as trusted markup.

commonMistakes: HttpOnly alone does not eliminate the impact of injected script.
guidedExercise: Compare text rendering with HTML insertion
material.independentExercise: Threat-model storing credentials where JavaScript can read them.
recallQuestions: What can a same-origin malicious script do?
Why does output context matter?

acceptanceCriteria: Untrusted content is not executed as markup
Credential-exposure risks are explained

topics.title: SameSite cookies
topics.description: SameSite controls cookie sending across site boundaries, which differ from origin boundaries.
learningGoals: Cookie policy supports the intended flow
Cross-site behavior is tested explicitly
examples: A user arrives through an external link.

tasks.title: Explain SameSite cookies in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: SameSite controls cookie sending across site boundaries, which differ from origin boundaries. Strict, Lax, and None allow different navigation and request behavior; None requires Secure. Validate the actual login and refresh flow instead of selecting a value mechanically.

workedExample.scenario: A user arrives through an external link.
steps: Strict may withhold a cookie.
Lax can behave differently for top-level safe navigation.

commonMistakes: Same-site and same-origin are not interchangeable concepts.
material.independentExercise: Choose attributes for a same-site app and document a cross-site alternative.
recallQuestions: What is the relevant site boundary?
Which user flow changes with Strict?

acceptanceCriteria: Cookie policy supports the intended flow
Cross-site behavior is tested explicitly

topics.title: Expiration
topics.description: Expiration limits credential usefulness over time.
learningGoals: Each credential has an explicit lifetime
Rotation respects the absolute session limit
examples: A session has an absolute expiry tomorrow.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Expiration limits credential usefulness over time. Distinguish access-token lifetime, refresh lifetime, and session idle or absolute limits. Rotation should not silently remove an absolute expiry policy by extending it forever.

workedExample.scenario: A session has an absolute expiry tomorrow.
steps: Refresh rotation creates a new token.
The replacement still respects the session deadline.

commonMistakes: New token issuance does not imply unlimited session lifetime.
guidedExercise: Draw access, refresh, and session timelines
material.independentExercise: Define expiration behavior after clock skew and prolonged inactivity.
recallQuestions: Which deadline survives rotation?
What happens exactly at expiry?

acceptanceCriteria: Each credential has an explicit lifetime
Rotation respects the absolute session limit

topics.title: Account enumeration and login throttling

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Authentication responses should avoid unnecessarily revealing whether an account exists.
learningGoals: Public responses minimize account disclosure
Abuse limits and recovery behavior are explicit
examples: Login fails for a missing user and a wrong password.

material.explanation: Authentication responses should avoid unnecessarily revealing whether an account exists. Use safe generic failure behavior and bounded throttling appropriate to the risk. Avoid turning account-based limits into an easy permanent denial of service.

workedExample.scenario: Login fails for a missing user and a wrong password.
steps: Return the same public failure category.
Record safe internal diagnostics and enforce bounded throttling.

commonMistakes: Different status or timing paths can reveal account existence.
material.independentExercise: Design password-reset request responses without confirming account existence.
recallQuestions: What information can reveal an account?
How can throttling be abused?

acceptanceCriteria: Public responses minimize account disclosure
Abuse limits and recovery behavior are explicit

exercises.title: Login Request
exercises.description: Describe login from request validation to safe credential issuance.
learningGoals: Describe login from request validation to safe credential issuance.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: A valid login authenticates U1.

tasks.title: Describe POST /login
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: Password verification uses a vetted policy
Verify: Failure responses minimize account disclosure
Verify: Credential transport and persistence are explicit
Verify: No password or raw token appears in logs

requirements: Specify POST /login request and response shapes
Validate input before credential verification
Use a vetted password verifier and generic public failure behavior
Create a session and issue credentials only after successful authentication
Define secure cookie or bearer transport explicitly
Apply bounded abuse protection and redact all credential values
constraints: Design first; no framework implementation required
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified
Request → authentication state → server actions → database actions → response

material.explanation: Trace the entire login operation rather than only its controller. Identify what state is created, what authority is returned, and where failures must remain generic. Password verification and token issuance have different secret-handling rules.

workedExample.scenario: A valid login authenticates U1.
steps: The server records session S1 and token verification state.
The client receives only the necessary credentials through the selected transport.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Compare wrong-password and missing-user public responses.
Label raw-secret locations and log exclusions.
material.independentExercise: Add a login-throttle policy and reason about deliberate lockout abuse.
recallQuestions: What persists after login?
What should an unauthenticated observer learn from failure?

acceptanceCriteria: Password verification uses a vetted policy
Failure responses minimize account disclosure
Credential transport and persistence are explicit
No password or raw token appears in logs

exercises.title: Refresh Request
exercises.description: Design refresh including replay and a response lost after commit.
learningGoals: Design refresh including replay and a response lost after commit.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: X rotates to Y and the transaction commits.

tasks.title: Describe POST /refresh
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: Only one child is created per parent
Verify: Reuse handling includes the active lineage policy
Verify: Lost responses have explicit client recovery
Verify: Refresh never bypasses absolute expiry or CSRF policy

requirements: Specify POST /refresh credential transport and response
Validate token, session, expiry, and revocation
Atomically consume the parent and persist its replacement
Define reuse detection and family or session revocation behavior
Document client recovery when rotation commits but the response is lost
Respect absolute session expiry and never persist raw tokens
constraints: Design first; do not claim a generic retry is safe
Evaluate browser CSRF defenses when cookies authenticate refresh
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified
State timeline for success, replay, and lost response

material.explanation: Refresh is a state transition with both security and reliability implications. A previously consumed token can represent theft or a legitimate retry; the server cannot simply know which. Choose a documented policy and explain its tradeoff.

workedExample.scenario: X rotates to Y and the transaction commits.
steps: The response carrying Y is lost.
A retry with X follows the declared reuse policy rather than issuing an accidental second child.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
material.independentExercise: Compare strict reuse rejection with a bounded retry protocol; explain any extra secret storage and attack exposure before selecting one.
recallQuestions: What evidence identifies a reuse attempt?
What does the client do after losing the replacement?

acceptanceCriteria: Only one child is created per parent
Reuse handling includes the active lineage policy
Lost responses have explicit client recovery
Refresh never bypasses absolute expiry or CSRF policy

exercises.title: Logout Request
exercises.description: Specify the exact guarantees of logout and logout-all.
learningGoals: Specify the exact guarantees of logout and logout-all.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: U1 owns S1 and S2.

tasks.title: Describe POST /logout
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: Single-session and all-session effects are distinct
Verify: Cross-user revocation is forbidden
Verify: Server revocation accompanies local cleanup
Verify: Access-token revocation limitations are documented

requirements: Define POST /logout and logout-all contracts
Use the trusted principal to identify allowed sessions
Revoke the intended server-side session and refresh family
Clear the relevant cookie under matching scope when applicable
Choose repeated-logout behavior
State whether previously issued access JWTs remain valid until expiration
constraints: Design first; do not promise immediate JWT revocation without a mechanism
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified

material.explanation: Logout affects server state and client-held credentials differently. Clearing a cookie alone does not revoke a stolen refresh value. Conversely, server revocation does not necessarily invalidate an offline-validated access JWT immediately.

workedExample.scenario: U1 owns S1 and S2.
steps: Logging out S1 revokes S1 but leaves S2 active.
Logout-all revokes both while respecting the access-token policy.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Trace cookie clearing and server revocation separately.
Specify repeated and already-expired logout behavior.
material.independentExercise: Write a user-facing guarantee that accurately describes remaining access-token validity.
recallQuestions: What remains after only clearing a cookie?
Which credential may survive server-side logout?
